facts.claim: "Breakfast in Bed" is a track on Dntel's 2007 album Dumb Luck, and Bright Eyes' Conor Oberst sings lead vocals on it.
Dumb Luck came out in the US on Sub Pop on April 24, 2007. Moshi Moshi Records issued the UK CD (moshicd19) on June 21, 2007.
The song runs 3:52 and is track 8 of 9 on Dumb Luck.
Tamborello says he met Oberst through Jenny Lewis, whom he worked with on The Postal Service album.
Tamborello told NME he had a song with no vocals and asked Oberst if he wanted to sing on it. Oberst came over and recorded it, which Tamborello called "all pretty casual".

Tamborello's method for Dntel songs is to send contributors blank instrumental tracks with no instructions. They write the lyrics and vocals themselves, and he wrote lyrics only for the title track "Dumb Luck".
Oberst said Tamborello asked him to sing on the song, that he loved the beat and an "Alka-Seltzer" sound in it, and that he thinks he recorded the vocals in Tamborello's LA apartment.
Tamborello said the main melodic loop on "Breakfast in Bed" was a simple synth line run through a Line 6 Delay Modeler with the dry signal removed.

Dumb Luck was written and recorded over about four to five years. Tamborello said he kept reworking the songs, and he later said the album had gone in a direction that was barely to his tastes by the time it was done.

Dntel is Jimmy Tamborello, a Los Angeles electronic producer who also works in The Postal Service with Ben Gibbard. He described Dumb Luck as "experimental techno-pop", and Dumb Luck followed 2001's Life Is Full of Possibilities as his third Dntel album.

research.lineage: Dntel's music is experimental techno-pop that blends electronic and organic instrumentation, and it sits in the indie-electronic scene around The Postal Service and the Rilo Kiley and Bright Eyes circle.

draft:
The tenderest line in **Breakfast In Bed** is also the bleakest. Near the end, the singer hopes the other person will always find someone to take them home, put them to bed, and hold a hand under their nose to make sure they're still breathing. That's love described as a wellness check. Then comes the admission: "I wish that could be me, but it's just not possible."

Conor Oberst sings it, and the words are his too. Jimmy Tamborello, who records as Dntel, sends collaborators blank instrumentals with no instructions and lets them write their own lyrics. He had a track with no vocals and asked Oberst if he wanted it. Oberst came over and recorded it, which Tamborello called "all pretty casual." Oberst thinks it happened in Tamborello's LA apartment. The two met through Jenny Lewis, whom Tamborello had worked with on The Postal Service album, and the song sits right in that overlap of laptop pop and the Bright Eyes and Rilo Kiley circle.

The scene is a morning after, somewhere away from home: wine in the coffee cup, birds outside, still drunk, the maids on their way. The narrator is giddy and wary at once. Last night the other person said they wanted to die, and now they want to live. They said they loved the narrator after forty-five minutes. The narrator sees all of it and signs on anyway: "If this is all a game can you just say it is? / I'll do it anyway." That's the knot of the song, clear eyes and total surrender in the same breath. Then the reason the morning has a clock on it is that back in New York nobody can find out. "We can say anything, but we just can't say it loud."

The music keeps that hush. A drum machine lays down a sparse, hip-hop-leaning beat with a firm snare, and the tempo is slow and unbothered. A synth pad holds the chords while a synth bass walks underneath. Tamborello has said the main melodic loop is a simple synth line run through a delay modeler with the dry signal removed, so what you hear is only the echo. That suits a song about a moment that's already turning into memory. Oberst said he loved the beat and an "Alka-Seltzer" sound in it. He stays breathy and close to the mic, almost conversational, with a second voice drifting in on harmony. The production is clean and polished, with a little reverb on the voice and nothing pushed.

It sticks because it lets you stand inside a hard kind of tenderness: caring for someone completely in a room you'll both have to leave before anyone back home notices.
